passages.original: Ergoetnomen verbum est, quandoqnidcm id videmus cum aliquo significatu articulata voce proferri; et cum dicimus disertum hominem bonis verbis uti, etiam nominibusnlique utitur; et cum seni domino apud Terentium servus retulit, Bona verba quælo (In Andria, act. i, 'cen. 2, v. 33), multa illc etiam nomina dixerat. Ad. Assentior. Aug. Concedis igitur iis duabus syllabis quas edimus, cum dicimus, Verbum, nomen quoque significari, et ob hoc illud hujus signum esse.
passages.english: Therefore a name is also a word, since we see that it is uttered with articulate voice with some meaning; and when we say that an eloquent man uses good words, he also uses names; and when in Terence the slave said to his old master, "Good words, I beg you" (Andria, act 1, scene 2, line 33), he had also spoken many names. Ad. I agree. Aug. You grant, then, that by these two syllables which we utter when we say "word" (verbum), "name" is also signified, and that for this reason the former is a sign of the latter.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'Ergoetnomen' = 'Ergo et nomen', 'nominibusnlique' = 'nominibus aliquis/utique', 'quælo' = 'quæso'). The phrase 'etiam nominibus [utique] utitur' is read as 'he certainly also uses names'.

passages.original: Verumtamen quia fieri potest ut ego illum locum nrinus bene intelligam, exponaturquc alias aliter, vel a ure vul ab alio ; est ad quod responderi pos.e nihil puto. Tradunt enim nobilissimi disputationum magisiri, nomine et verbo plenam constare sententiam, quan afirmari negarique possit : quod genus idem Tullius quodam loco pronuntiatum vocat : et cum verbi tertia persona est, nominativum cum ea casun. nominis aiunt esse oportere; et recte aiunt : quod mecum si consideres, velut cum dicimus, nomo sedet, Equus currit, agnoscis , ut opinor, duo esse pronuntiata.
passages.english: Nevertheless, because it may happen that I understand that passage less well, and that it is explained otherwise by me or by someone else, there is [another point] to which I think no reply can be made. For the most distinguished masters of disputation teach that a complete sentence, which can be affirmed or denied, consists of a name and a verb; this kind [of sentence] the same Tullius in a certain place calls a "proposition" (pronuntiatum); and they say that when the verb is in the third person, the name with it must be in the nominative case; and they say rightly. If you consider this with me, as when we say "A man sits," "A horse runs," you recognize, I think, that there are two propositions.
passages.notes: Many scanning errors corrected: 'nrinus' = 'minus', 'a ure vul ab alio' = 'a me vel ab alio', 'pos.e' = 'posse', 'quan afirmari' = 'quae affirmari', 'casun.' = 'casum', 'nomo' = 'homo'. 'Nomen' and 'verbum' here are grammatical terms, 'noun' and 'verb'; rendered 'name' for consistency with the dialogue.

passages.original: cnm ipsius cognitio nominis multo sit inferior cognitione vitiorum. Licet itque constituas etiam ista quatuor atque consideres, nomen et rem, cognitionem nominis et cognitionem rei; primum secundo jure præponimus. Huc enim positum nomcn in carmine, cum ait Persius, Sed stupet hic vitio (Satyra 3, v. 32), non modo nibil vitii fecit in versu , sed nomihil etiam ornatus dedit: cnm tamen res ipsa quæ signilicatur hoc nomine, in quocumque inest, cogat esse vitiosum.
passages.english: since knowledge of the name itself is far inferior to knowledge of vices. So even if you set up these four and consider them, the name and the thing, knowledge of the name and knowledge of the thing, we rightly place the first before the second. For this name, placed in a poem when Persius says, "But this man is stupefied by vice" (Satire 3, line 32), not only caused no fault in the verse but even gave it some ornament; whereas the thing itself which is signified by this name compels whoever it is in to be vicious.
passages.notes: The opening clause begins mid-sentence; its sense depends on preceding context. Scanning errors corrected ('Licet itque' = 'Licet itaque', 'Huc' = 'Hoc', 'nomihil' = 'nonnihil'). The first sentence, as transmitted, seems to argue the reverse of the following one; the logic fits a reading in which the name is ranked above the thing, and knowledge of the thing above knowledge of the name.
